gold_decisions.identity_explanation: ISSUE-006 identifies sign errors in differentiating the optimized MMD expression and in the intermediate gradient proof. Gold I001 concerns a factor-of-two normalization mismatch between the definition of G_M and the Lloyd gradient, repaired by halving the squared Wasserstein objective. These are distinct formula defects despite both affecting a gradient derivation.

Both entries identify the missing nonsingularity/invertibility hypothesis needed before using K(Y)^{-1} and the resulting inverse-based weights and gradient formulas. ISSUE-001 also recognizes that the affected downstream corollary requires the corresponding relevant Gram matrix to be invertible, covering the one-particle diagonal case described in the gold repair.
gold_decisions.shared_mathematical_weakness: The theorem and its dependent formulas use inverse-based kernel/Gram-matrix weights without assuming that the relevant matrices are nonsingular; admissible singular configurations therefore make the weights, differentiation calculation, and one-particle quotient undefined.

component_coverage.gold_component: Missing nonsingularity domain condition for K(Y)^{-1}-based theorem weights and differentiation, including the singular-kernel counterexample and restriction to invertible Gram configurations.
component_coverage.recognition_explanation: ISSUE-001 explicitly states that no nonsingularity assumption is imposed, gives a singular Gram-matrix example under the stated kernel assumptions, identifies the inverse construction and later gradient uses as undefined or unsupported, and proposes restricting to invertible matrices or using a nonunique/pseudoinverse formulation.

component_coverage.gold_component: Propagation of the same missing invertibility condition to the one-particle quotient involving kappa(y,y).
component_coverage.recognition_explanation: ISSUE-001 identifies the downstream gradient and corollary formulas as relying on the inverse-based weights and calls for invertibility of all relevant Gram matrices, which includes the one-point Gram matrix; its effect and repair therefore recognize the same missing domain requirement rather than merely sharing the theorem location.
